prompt: What does a CRDT guarantee about two copies that have received the same updates?

choices.text: That they hold what the person meant
choices.why: Intent is exactly what it does not promise.

choices.text: That a server approved every update
choices.why: No server has to decide anything.

choices.text: That they are in the same state, whatever the order
choices.why: Right. That is strong eventual consistency.

choices.text: That no update was delivered twice
choices.why: Repeats may happen; idempotence makes them harmless.

prompt: Match each property of the merge to the sync problem it removes.

pairs.right: devices sync in whatever order they find a network
updates travel through other devices, in groups
a retry delivers the same update again

right_distractors: two devices set the same field to different values

prompt: Two devices set the same field of a CRDT to different values at the same time. What happens?

choices.text: A fixed rule keeps one, the same on every device
choices.why: Right. Last write wins with a better tie-break, not a reading of intent.

choices.text: Both values are kept, side by side, in that field forever
choices.why: A register keeps one value; a fixed rule picks it.

choices.text: The merge fails until a person chooses
choices.why: A CRDT merge never fails; that is its point.

choices.text: The device that synced last wins
choices.why: The order of syncing makes no difference to a CRDT.

prompt: Why does the grow-only counter never lose an increment?

choices.text: It keeps the newest total by timestamp
choices.why: That is last write wins, which lost 45 minutes.

choices.text: The server adds the totals the devices send
choices.why: Adding totals counts the shared 100 twice; lesson 13's totals were the problem.

choices.text: It locks the counter while a device adds to it
choices.why: There is no lock anywhere in a CRDT.

choices.text: Each device writes only its own entry
choices.why: Right. Nothing overwrites anything, so the merge keeps every count.

prompt: A G-counter reads {phone: 60, tablet: 40}. Offline, the phone adds 30 and the tablet adds 45. What is the total after the two copies merge?
The merge of two G-counters keeps, for each device, which count?

choices.text: The sum of the two copies' counts
choices.why: Summing would count a shared entry twice, and merging twice would add it again.

choices.text: The larger one
choices.why: Right. A device's own count only grows, so the larger is the later.

choices.text: The newer one
choices.why: Counts carry no time; none is needed.

choices.text: The phone's, because it was created first
choices.why: No device ranks above another.

prompt: In the run, the phone re-adds `weekly` with tag p2 while the tablet removes `weekly`. Why does `weekly` stay?

choices.text: The phone's change arrived later
choices.why: Arrival order does not matter; the run merged both ways.

choices.text: The tablet's remove covered only a1, the tag it had seen
choices.why: Right. p2 was never observed by the remover, so it survives.

choices.text: Adds are applied after removes in the merge function
choices.why: mergeSet takes two unions; nothing is applied in an order.

choices.text: Sets keep every value ever added
choices.why: `weekly` with tag a1 alone would have been removed.

prompt: A study budget allows 120 minutes a week. Two offline devices each record the last 20 minutes against it. What does the lesson say a CRDT can do about it?

choices.text: A PN-counter refuses the second 20 minutes
choices.why: A PN-counter adds and subtracts; it refuses nothing.

choices.text: An OR-set removes one of the two records
choices.why: No merge removes something nobody asked to remove.

choices.text: A G-counter caps itself at 120
choices.why: Its merge is a maximum per device; it has no cap.

choices.text: Nothing: refusing it is a server's job
choices.why: Right. A rule across all devices needs one place that says yes or no.

prompt: What does a device send in Yjs so that the other sends back only what is missing?

choices.text: Its state vector
choices.why: Right. It says what this copy has already seen.

choices.text: Its whole document
choices.why: That is what the state vector saves them from.

choices.text: A timestamp of its last sync
choices.why: Yjs reads no clock to sync.

choices.text: A version number per row
choices.why: That is lesson 14's mechanism, not Yjs's.

prompt: In the first Yjs run, why did 30 minutes and done both survive?

choices.text: Yjs asked which value to keep
choices.why: Nothing was asked; there was no question.

choices.text: The phone synced after the tablet
choices.why: Order does not matter in a CRDT merge.

choices.text: s3 is a nested Y.Map, so each field is its own key
choices.why: Right. Each field has its own history, and they never competed.

choices.text: Yjs kept a base copy, as lesson 14 does
choices.why: No base copy was kept; the separation came from the data's shape.

prompt: Both devices change s3's minutes in a Yjs document, to 30 and to 25. What does the lesson say the app has to do if Ana should choose?

choices.text: Notice the case itself
choices.why: Right. Yjs settled it with a tie-break and moved on.

choices.text: Read the conflict Yjs records in the document
choices.why: Nothing in the document says a conflict happened.

choices.text: Turn on Yjs's conflict mode before syncing
choices.why: The lesson names no such mode; a CRDT does not stop to ask.

choices.text: Nothing: Yjs keeps both values in the field until somebody picks one
choices.why: Both devices showed 25 and the 30 was gone.

prompt: An app can store a whole Yjs document in SQLite as the bytes of `Y.encodeStateAsUpdate(doc)`, in a column of type ___.
In the lesson's run with garbage collection off, how many bytes did the Yjs document weigh after the thousand notes were added and deleted?
Why would an app turn Yjs's garbage collection off, knowing the cost?

choices.text: Syncing is faster without it
choices.why: The run measured size, and the updates grew.

choices.text: Without it, two devices can no longer merge
choices.why: They merge either way; collection decides what is kept.

choices.text: To offer undo or show an earlier version
choices.why: Right. Both need the deleted content to still be there.

choices.text: Because SQLite cannot store a collected document
choices.why: Either document is just bytes in a BLOB.

prompt: For which of these is a CRDT the wrong tool, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the last free seat in a live class
choices.why: A rule across all devices needs a server that can refuse.

choices.text: a report over every student's minutes
choices.why: Bytes in a BLOB cannot be queried with SQL.

choices.text: shared notes two classmates type into
choices.why: That is the case CRDTs are for.

choices.text: minutes studied, added from two devices
choices.why: A counter where every addition counts is a CRDT's strength.

prompt: A team wants to move the planner's sessions into a Yjs document to avoid conflict screens. What does the lesson warn they lose?

choices.text: Convergence: two devices may disagree forever
choices.why: Convergence is exactly what Yjs guarantees.

choices.text: The same-field case, now settled in silence
choices.why: Right. Lesson 14 kept it for the person; a CRDT picks one.

choices.text: Offline editing, since Yjs needs a server to merge
choices.why: Yjs merged two offline copies with no server at all.

choices.text: The notes, which Yjs cannot merge
choices.why: The notes merged perfectly in the run.

prompt: Put a Yjs sync between the phone and the tablet in order, as the lesson's program does it.
items: each device edits its own copy offline
each encodes, for the other, the updates missing from that vector
each applies the update it received

prompt: Which part of the planner does the lesson suggest giving to a CRDT?

choices.text: The sessions, with their minutes and done fields
choices.why: Lesson 14's versions suit them, and keep the conflicts visible.

choices.text: The whole planner, as one document per account
choices.why: The server could no longer query it or refuse a write.

choices.text: The list of courses and their names
choices.why: A name is replaced whole; lesson 13's rule is enough there.

choices.text: The notes and the minutes studied
choices.why: Right. A shared list and a counter where every addition counts.
